topics.title: Systematic curve sketching with the derivative

questions.stem: The diagram shows a curve \( y = f(x) \) with turning points at \( (-2, -4) \) and \( (3, 6) \), and a point of inflection at \( (0.5, 1) \). Determine the properties of the curve from this graph.

parts.stem: a) Find the values of \( x \) for which \( f'(x) = 0 \). (If there are multiple values, list them in ascending order, separated by a comma.)

steps.explain: Recall the definition of a turning point.
steps.work: \text{At a turning point, the gradient is zero, so } f'(x) = 0.

steps.explain: Identify the x-coordinates of the turning points from the given information.
steps.work: \text{The turning points are at } (-2, -4) \text{ and } (3, 6). \text{ Thus, } f'(x) = 0 \text{ at } x = -2 \text{ and } x = 3.

parts.stem: b) Find the value of \( x \) for which \( f''(x) = 0 \).

steps.explain: Recall the definition of a point of inflection.
steps.work: \text{At a possible point of inflection, the second derivative } f''(x) = 0.

steps.explain: Identify the x-coordinate of the point of inflection from the given information.
steps.work: \text{The point of inflection is at } (0.5, 1). \text{ Thus, } f''(x) = 0 \text{ at } x = 0.5.

parts.stem: c) State the interval of \( x \) for which \( f(x) \) is increasing. (Format: 'a < x < b')

steps.explain: Relate increasing behavior to the turning points.
steps.work: \text{The function is increasing when } f'(x) > 0. \text{ The curve goes from a minimum at } (-2, -4) \text{ up to a maximum at } (3, 6).
\text{Between } x = -2 \text{ and } x = 3 \text{, the graph is rising. Therefore, it is increasing for } -2 < x < 3.

parts.stem: d) State the interval of \( x \) for which the curve is concave up, that is \( f''(x) > 0 \).

steps.explain: Relate concavity to the second derivative and inflection point.
steps.work: \text{Concave up means } f''(x) > 0. \text{ Concavity changes at the point of inflection } x = 0.5.

steps.explain: Determine concavity on each side of the inflection point.
steps.work: \text{The turning point at } x = -2 \text{ is a local minimum, which sits in a concave up region (} f''(-2) > 0 \text{).} \\ \text{The turning point at } x = 3 \text{ is a local maximum, which sits in a concave down region (} f''(3) < 0 \text{).}
\text{The curve is concave up before the inflection point, so for } x < 0.5.

questions.stem: For the parabola \( y = x^2 - 4x - 12 \), complete the following analysis steps.

parts.stem: a) Find the \( x \)-intercepts of the parabola. (If there are multiple values, list them in ascending order, separated by a comma.)

steps.explain: Set \( y = 0 \) to find the x-intercepts.

parts.stem: b) By putting \( x = 0 \, \), find the \( y \)-intercept.
c) Solve \( \frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \) and hence find the coordinates of the stationary point.
d) By examining the sign of \( \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \), state whether the stationary point is a maximum or a minimum.

steps.explain: Evaluate the sign of the second derivative.
steps.work: \text{Since } \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2 > 0 \text{ for all } x \text{, the curve is concave up everywhere.}
\text{Therefore, the stationary point is a minimum.}

parts.stem: e) Sketch the graph of the function, indicating all important features.
parts.answer: Draw a concave up parabola with vertex at (2,-16), x-intercepts at -2 and 6, and y-intercept at -12.

steps.work: \text{Mark the points } (-2, 0) \text{ and } (6, 0) \text{ on the x-axis.}
\text{Draw a smooth, concave up parabolic curve passing through all these points.}

questions.stem: Sketch the following quadratic graphs, indicating all intercepts and turning points.

parts.stem: a) Sketch the graph of \( y = x^2 - 6x \).
parts.answer: A concave up parabola with vertex at (3,-9), passing through (0,0) and (6,0).

steps.work: \text{Plot the vertex } (3, -9) \text{ and intercepts } (0,0), (6,0) \text{. Draw a concave up parabola.}

parts.stem: b) Sketch the graph of \( y = 8 - 2x - x^2 \).
parts.answer: A concave down parabola with vertex at (-1,9), passing through (-4,0), (2,0), and (0,8).

steps.work: \text{Plot the vertex } (-1, 9) \text{ and intercepts } (0,8), (-4,0), (2,0) \text{. Draw a concave down parabola.}

questions.stem: For the function \( y = 12x - x^3 \), perform a complete calculus analysis to sketch its graph.

parts.stem: a) Show that \( y = 12x - x^3 \) is an odd function. What symmetry does its graph display?
options: It is odd because \( f(-x) = f(x) \). The graph displays line symmetry about the y-axis.
It is odd because \( f(-x) = -f(x) \). The graph displays line symmetry about the x-axis.
It is odd because \( f(-x) = f(x) \). The graph displays rotational point symmetry about the origin.
It is odd because \( f(-x) = -f(x) \). The graph displays rotational point symmetry of 180 degrees about the origin.

steps.explain: Substitute \( -x \) into the function to check for parity.

steps.work: \text{Since } f(-x) = -f(x) \text{, the function is odd. Odd functions have rotational point symmetry of } 180^{\circ} \text{ about the origin.}

parts.stem: b) Which of the following correctly gives the first and second derivatives of \( y = 12x - x^3 \)?
c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature. (Format: '(-2,-16) is a minimum, (2,16) is a maximum')
options: \( (-2, 16) \) is a minimum, \( (2, -16) \) is a maximum
\( (0, 0) \) is a minimum, \( (2, 16) \) is a maximum
\( (-2, -16) \) is a minimum, \( (2, 16) \) is a maximum
\( (-2, -16) \) is a maximum, \( (2, 16) \) is a minimum

steps.explain: Set \( y' = 0 \) to find the stationary points.

steps.work: \begin{aligned} y''(2) &= -6(2) = -12 < 0 \implies (2, 16) \text{ is a maximum} \\ y''(-2) &= -6(-2) = 12 > 0 \implies (-2, -16) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}

parts.stem: d) Why is \( x = 0 \) a point of inflection?
options: Because \( y' = 0 \) at \( x = 0 \) and the sign of \( y' \) changes across it.
Because \( y'' = 0 \) at \( x = 0 \) and the sign of \( y'' \) changes across it.
Because \( y'' = 0 \) at \( x = 0 \) and \( y'' \) remains positive on both sides.

steps.explain: Check if the second derivative is zero.
Test values around \( x = 0 \) to check for a change in concavity.
steps.work: \begin{aligned} \text{For } x < 0 \; (\text{e.g., } x = -1): y''(-1) &= -6(-1) = 6 > 0 \; (\text{Concave up}) \\ \text{For } x > 0 \; (\text{e.g., } x = 1): y''(1) &= -6(1) = -6 < 0 \; (\text{Concave down}) \end{aligned}
\text{Since } y'' \text{ changes sign across } x = 0 \text{, it is a point of inflection.}

parts.stem: e) By substituting into the gradient function \( y' \), find the gradient at the inflection point.

steps.explain: Substitute the x-coordinate of the inflection point into the gradient function.

parts.stem: f) Sketch the graph of the function, indicating all important features.
parts.answer: Cubic curve with minimum at (-2,-16), maximum at (2,16), inflection at (0,0), and x-intercepts at 0, \pm 2\sqrt{3}.

steps.work: \text{Mark the origin } (0, 0) \text{ which is the inflection point.}
\text{Mark the minimum at } (-2, -16) \text{ and the maximum at } (2, 16).

\text{Draw a smooth curve through the points. Since it's an odd cubic with a negative leading coefficient, it comes from } +\infty \text{ in the 2nd quadrant, goes down to the minimum, passes through the origin, goes up to the maximum, and goes down to } -\infty \text{ in the 4th quadrant.}

questions.stem: For the curve \( f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12 \), perform a complete calculus analysis to sketch its graph.

parts.stem: a) Which of the following correctly gives the first and second derivatives of \( f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12 \)?
b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature. (Format: '(0,12) is a maximum, (3,-15) is a minimum')
options: \( (0, 12) \) is a maximum, \( (3, -15) \) is a minimum
\( (0, -12) \) is a maximum, \( (3, 15) \) is a minimum
\( (0, 12) \) is a maximum, \( (3, 15) \) is a minimum
\( (0, 12) \) is a minimum, \( (3, -15) \) is a maximum

steps.explain: Set \( f'(x) = 0 \) to find the stationary points.

steps.work: \begin{aligned} f''(0) &= -18 < 0 \implies (0, 12) \text{ is a maximum} \\ f''(3) &= 12(3) - 18 = 36 - 18 = 18 > 0 \implies (3, -15) \text{ is a minimum} \end{aligned}

parts.stem: c) Explain why there is a point of inflection at \( x = 1.5 \), and find the gradient at the inflection point.
options: Since \( f''(1.5) = 0 \) and concavity changes, it is an inflection point with gradient \( -13.5 \).
Since \( f''(1.5) = 0 \) and concavity changes, it is an inflection point with gradient \( 13.5 \).
Since \( f'(1.5) = 0 \), it is a stationary point with gradient \( 0 \).
Since \( f''(1.5) = 0 \) and concavity does not change, it is not an inflection point.

steps.explain: Evaluate the second derivative at \( x = 1.5 \).

steps.work: \begin{aligned} \text{For } x < 1.5, f''(x) < 0 \text{ (concave down).} \\ \text{For } x > 1.5, f''(x) > 0 \text{ (concave up).} \\ \implies \text{Concavity changes, so it is an inflection point.} \end{aligned}

parts.stem: d) Sketch the graph of \( f(x) \), indicating all important features.
parts.answer: Cubic curve with local maximum at (0,12), local minimum at (3,-15), and point of inflection at (1.5, -1.5).

steps.work: \text{Mark the maximum at } (0, 12) \text{ and the minimum at } (3, -15).
\text{Draw a smooth cubic curve that comes from } -\infty \text{, reaches the maximum on the y-axis, passes through the inflection point, hits the minimum, and goes off to } +\infty.

questions.stem: For the quartic curve \( y = 4x^3 - x^4 + 5 \), perform a calculus analysis to sketch its graph.

parts.stem: a) Which of the following correctly gives the first and second derivatives of \( y = 4x^3 - x^4 + 5 \)?
b) By solving \( y' = 0 \), find the coordinates of any stationary points. (List points in ascending order of x, e.g. '(0,5), (3,32)')

steps.explain: Set \( y' = 0 \) to find stationary points.

parts.stem: c) By examining the sign of \( y'' \), establish the nature of the stationary point at \( x = 3 \). Why does this method fail for the stationary point at \( x = 0 \)?
options: \( (3, 32) \) is a local maximum because \( y''(3) = -36 < 0 \). The method fails at \( x = 0 \) because \( y''(0) = 0 \).
\( (3, 32) \) is a local minimum because \( y''(3) = 36 > 0 \). The method fails at \( x = 0 \) because \( y''(0) = 0 \).
\( (3, 32) \) is a local maximum because \( y''(3) = -36 < 0 \). The method fails at \( x = 0 \) because \( y'(0) = 0 \).
\( (3, 32) \) is a point of inflection because \( y''(3) = 0 \).

steps.explain: Evaluate the second derivative at \( x = 3 \).

steps.work: \text{Since } y''(3) < 0 \text{, the point } (3, 32) \text{ is a local maximum.}

steps.explain: Evaluate the second derivative at \( x = 0 \).

steps.work: \text{The second derivative test is inconclusive when } y'' = 0. \text{ We must use the first derivative test to determine its nature.}

parts.stem: d) Use a table of test values of \( y' \) to show that there is a stationary point of inflection at \( x = 0 \).
options: The slope is negative on both sides of \( x = 0 \), indicating a horizontal point of inflection.
The slope is positive on both sides of \( x = 0 \) (\( y' > 0 \)), indicating it is a horizontal point of inflection.
The slope changes from positive to negative, indicating a maximum.
The slope changes from negative to positive, indicating a minimum.

steps.explain: Use test values around \( x = 0 \) in the first derivative \( y' = 4x^2(3 - x) \).

steps.work: \text{Since the gradient is positive before and after } x = 0 \text{, the curve flattens out but continues to rise. Thus, } (0, 5) \text{ is a horizontal (stationary) point of inflection.}

parts.stem: e) Why is there a change in concavity at \( x = 2 \)?
options: Because \( y' = 0 \) at \( x = 2 \) and changes sign across it.
Because \( y'' = 0 \) at \( x = 2 \) and changes sign from negative to positive across it.
Because \( y'' = 0 \) at \( x = 2 \) and changes sign from positive to negative across it.

steps.explain: Check the second derivative at \( x = 2 \).
Test values around \( x = 2 \) in \( y'' = 12x(2 - x) \).
steps.work: \begin{aligned} \text{For } x = 1: y''(1) &= 12(1)(2 - 1) = 12 > 0 \; (\text{Concave up}) \\ \text{For } x = 3: y''(3) &= 12(3)(2 - 3) = -36 < 0 \; (\text{Concave down}) \end{aligned}
\text{Since } y'' \text{ changes from positive to negative across } x = 2 \text{, there is a change in concavity, making it a point of inflection.}

parts.stem: f) Sketch the graph of the function, showing all important features.
parts.answer: Quartic curve with local maximum at (3,32), horizontal point of inflection at (0,5), and non-stationary point of inflection at (2,21).

steps.work: \text{Mark the horizontal point of inflection at } (0, 5) \text{ and the maximum at } (3, 32).

steps.explain: Plot the non-stationary point of inflection.

steps.work: \text{Draw a smooth curve rising from the left, flattening at } (0, 5) \text{, continuing to rise through } (2, 21) \text{ to reach the peak at } (3, 32) \text{, and then falling rapidly to the right.}

questions.stem: For the rational function \( y = x + \frac{4}{x} \), complete the following systematic curve sketching analysis.

parts.stem: a) Show that the derivative of \( y = x + \frac{4}{x} \) is \( y' = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x^2} \).
b) Find the stationary points and determine their nature. (Format: '(-2,-4) is a maximum, (2,4) is a minimum')
options: \( (2, 4) \) is a maximum, \( (-2, -4) \) is a minimum
\( (-2, -4) \) is an inflection point, \( (2, 4) \) is an inflection point
\( (-2, -4) \) is a maximum, \( (2, 4) \) is a minimum
\( (-2, -4) \) is a minimum, \( (2, 4) \) is a maximum

steps.explain: Set \( y' = 0 \) to find stationary points.
Find second derivative to determine nature.

steps.work: \begin{aligned} y''(2) &= \frac{8}{8} = 1 > 0 \implies (2, 4) \text{ is a minimum} \\ y''(-2) &= \frac{8}{-8} = -1 < 0 \implies (-2, -4) \text{ is a maximum} \end{aligned}

parts.stem: c) Show that the function is odd. What symmetry does its graph have?
options: The function is even and displays line symmetry about the y-axis.
The function is neither even nor odd.
The function is odd and displays rotational point symmetry of 180 degrees about the origin.
The function is odd and displays line symmetry about the y-axis.

steps.work: \text{Since } f(-x) = -f(x) \text{, the function is odd and has rotational symmetry about the origin.}

parts.stem: d) State the domain of the function and the equation of the vertical asymptote. (Format: 'domain: x not equal to 0; vertical asymptote: x = 0')
options: domain: all real \( x \); no vertical asymptote

steps.explain: Find where the function is undefined.

steps.work: \text{The domain is all real } x \neq 0 \text{, and the vertical asymptote is } x = 0.

parts.stem: e) Use a table of test values of \( y \) to analyse the sign of the function.
parts.answer: For x < 0, y < 0. For x > 0, y > 0.

steps.explain: Analyze the sign on either side of the asymptote.
steps.work: \begin{aligned} \text{For } x < 0 \text{ (e.g., } x = -1), y &= -1 - 4 = -5 < 0 \\ \text{For } x > 0 \text{ (e.g., } x = 1), y &= 1 + 4 = 5 > 0 \end{aligned}

parts.stem: f) Sketch the graph of the function. (You may assume that the diagonal line \( y = x \) is an oblique asymptote to the curve.)
parts.answer: Sketch curve with vertical asymptote at x = 0 and oblique asymptote at y = x, with a local maximum at (-2,-4) and a local minimum at (2,4).

steps.work: \text{Draw dashed line for } x=0 \text{ (y-axis) and } y = x.
\text{Draw a hyperbola-like curve approaching the asymptotes, with vertices at the turning points.}

parts.stem: g) Write down the range of the function. (Format: 'y <= -4 or y >= 4')

steps.work: \text{The left branch peaks at } y = -4 \text{, so it covers } y \le -4. \text{ The right branch has its lowest point at } y = 4 \text{, so it covers } y \ge 4.
